title: Doomscrolling at work wastes time, but the real cost is its lingering psychological effects
summary: A study by Texas A&M University reveals that doomscrolling—obsessively consuming negative news during work—reduces employee engagement due to prolonged rumination on distressing content. The research, published in *Computers in Human Behavior*, highlights that this behavior is particularly harmful to individuals with higher neuroticism and extends beyond mere productivity loss, impacting mental focus and workplace performance. While doomscrolling stems from a desire to stay informed, it often leads to persistent negative thoughts. Experts suggest setting boundaries, such as confining doomscrolling to specific locations, rather than enforcing strict workplace bans.
key_points: Doomscrolling at work leads to rumination on negative news, reducing work engagement.
The study involved workers in the U.S. and U.K., showing consistent patterns across regions.
Employees with higher neuroticism are more vulnerable to the effects of doomscrolling.
Doomscrolling is an information-seeking behavior driven by uncertainty, not just mindless scrolling.
Modern workplaces exacerbate the issue due to constant access to news via smartphones and laptops.
Experts recommend setting boundaries (e.g., confining doomscrolling to specific locations) rather than strict bans.
The behavior is likely to persist due to algorithm-driven social media and expanding digital access.
